text: Causes of Pasture Decline | 🌿 1. Overgrazing | What it is: | Overgrazing happens when animals stay in a paddock for too long and eat plants faster than they can regrow. | Why it's a problem: | Leaves plants weakened or dead | Exposes bare soil to wind and water | Increases risk of erosion and weed invasion | Reduces long-term pasture productivity | Common signs: | Short, patchy grass; visible bare soil; hoof damage

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/2. Pastures & Cropping/5.1 Managing Pasture Deterioration.pptx
text: Causes of Pasture Decline | 🌿 | 2. Understocking | What it is: | Too few animals grazing a paddock, or leaving paddocks ungrazed for long periods. | Why it's a problem: | Grass becomes over-mature ("rank") and loses feed value | Ungrazed pasture can shade out younger plants | Weeds and unpalatable species spread due to lack of grazing pressure | Common signs: | Tall, woody pasture with seed heads; weeds taking over

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/2. Pastures & Cropping/5.1 Managing Pasture Deterioration.pptx
text: Causes of Pasture Decline | 🌿 3. | Selective Grazing | What it is: | Animals consistently eat only the most palatable (tasty) plants and avoid others. | Why it's a problem: | Desirable species (like ryegrass or clover) are removed | Less palatable species (like weeds or thistles) are left to spread | Reduces pasture quality and biodiversity over time | Common signs: | Patchy grazing; some plants heavily eaten, others untouched

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/2. Pastures & Cropping/5.1 Managing Pasture Deterioration.pptx
text: Causes of Pasture Decline | 🌿 | 4. Soil Compaction | What it is: | When soil becomes densely packed due to trampling (by livestock) or machinery, especially when wet. | Why it's a problem: | Roots can’t penetrate compacted layers | Reduces air and water movement in the soil | Leads to poor growth and water runoff instead of absorption | Common signs: | Pooled water, stunted plants, hard soil surface, hoof prints in wet ground

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/2. Pastures & Cropping/5.1 Managing Pasture Deterioration.pptx
text: Causes of Pasture Decline | 🌿 | 5. Pest Infestation | What it is: | Pests such as red-legged earth mites, lucerne flea, or insect larvae damage pasture plants, especially seedlings. | Why it's a problem: | Reduces ground cover | Weakens plant health | Slows or stops regrowth after grazing or drought | Common signs: | Patchy areas with chewed leaves, discoloured grass, or dead patches

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/2. Pastures & Cropping/5.1 Managing Pasture Deterioration.pptx
text: Causes of Pasture Decline | 🌿 6. Lack of Rotation | What it is: | Grazing the same paddock with no rest or crop rotation for extended periods. | Why it's a problem: | Nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus are used up | Soil structure can degrade | Weed and pest pressure builds up | Common signs: | Low fertility, uneven growth, poor response to fertiliser

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/2. Pastures & Cropping/5.1 Managing Pasture Deterioration.pptx
text: 🌾Management Strategies to Prevent or Reverse Decline | Strategy | What It Does | Rotational grazing | Moves animals between paddocks → allows regrowth → maintains cover and species balance | Reseeding/Oversowing | Replaces lost pasture species → improves density and competitiveness against weeds | Soil amendments | Lime corrects pH, fertiliser restores nutrients → supports healthy plant growth | Fallowing paddocks | Leaving a paddock ungrazed for a season → restores soil and plant condition | Pest management | Targeted control (e.g., for red-legged earth mites) → protects seedling survival

text: 🐑  Pregnancy Scanning | What it is: | Using ultrasound to detect pregnancies and determine litter size (single, twin, or triplet). | When | : About | 6–8 weeks after rams are removed | . | How | : A trained operator uses a portable ultrasound scanner on the ewe’s belly. | Why important: | Helps separate and feed ewes according to needs — ewes carrying twins need more nutrition than those carrying singles. | Example | : A farmer scans in Late May-June to plan supplementary feeding for twin-bearing ewes.

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/3. Prime Lamb Production/5.1 Prime Lamb Management Calendar.pptx
text: 🐑 | Lambing | What it is | : The period when ewes give birth to lambs. | When | : Usually | August–September | in Wagga-based enterprises. | How | : Ewes are placed in safe paddocks with shelter; farmers check daily for mismothering, lamb losses, or birthing difficulties. | Why important | : Survival of lambs is critical to profitability; good lambing management increases weaning percentages. | Example | : A paddock with tree lines and long grass provides protection from cold winds, improving lamb survival rates.

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/3. Prime Lamb Production/5.1 Prime Lamb Management Calendar.pptx
text: 🐑 | Lamb Marking | What it is | : Husbandry procedures performed on lambs at | 2–6 weeks old | : tail docking, castration, and vaccination. | When | : Spring, shortly after lambing. | How | : Lambs are mustered with their mothers, marked quickly and humanely, and returned to the mob. | Why important | : Tail docking reduces flystrike risk, castration controls breeding in unwanted males, vaccinations protect from diseases like tetanus. | Example | : A producer marks all lambs in October, giving a 5-in-1 vaccine to protect against clostridial diseases.

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/3. Prime Lamb Production/5.1 Prime Lamb Management Calendar.pptx
text: 🐑 | Weaning | What it is | : Separating lambs from their mothers so both can feed independently. | When | : About | 3–4 months after lambing. | How | : Lambs are moved to separate paddocks with quality feed, and ewes are allowed to recover body condition before the next joining. | Why important | : Allows targeted feeding of lambs for growth and of ewes for recovery; also reduces parasite transfer from ewe to lamb. | Example | : Weaning in | November | allows lambs to graze fresh summer pastures and ewes to prepare for autumn joining.

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/3. Prime Lamb Production/5.1 Prime Lamb Management Calendar.pptx
text: 🐑 | Shearing | What it is | : Removing the wool from sheep. | When | : Once a year (varies by enterprise) — for prime lamb producers, often after weaning. | How | : Sheep are shorn by professional shearers using electric handpieces; wool is classed and baled. | Why important | : Prevents heat stress and flystrike, and produces a marketable wool product. Timing also affects wool quality (length, cleanliness). | Example | : A mixed farm shears in | November-December | after lambs are weaned so sheep go into summer with less fleece, reducing flystrike risk.

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/3. Prime Lamb Production/5.1 Prime Lamb Management Calendar.pptx
text: 🐑 | Drenching / Vaccinations | What it is | : Administering treatments to prevent internal parasites and protect from disease. | When | : Several times a year, especially at high-risk times (after lamb marking, at weaning, before joining). | How | : Oral drenches for worms; injectable or oral vaccines for diseases. | Why important: | Healthy sheep grow faster, produce more, and have better welfare outcomes. | Example | : Ewes are drenched pre-joining to prevent worm burdens from affecting fertility.

drivePath: /2026/Teaching and Learning Programs/3. Prime Lamb Production/5.1 Prime Lamb Management Calendar.pptx
text: 🐑 | Culling | What it is | : Removing unproductive, old, or unhealthy sheep from the flock. | When | : Often at weaning or before joining. | How | : Assessing body condition, teeth, udders, and production history; selling to market or abattoir. | Why important: | Keeps flock genetics strong, reduces feed costs on unproductive animals, and improves overall performance. | Example | : A farmer culls ewes with worn teeth after weaning so they don’t struggle to maintain condition.

text: Case Study 1: Beneficial Microorganisms - Rhizobium Bacteria | Overview: | Rhizobium bacteria are essential for the growth of legumes such as beans, peas, and lentils. These microorganisms form a symbiotic relationship with the roots of leguminous plants, where they fix nitrogen from the atmosphere into a form that plants can use. In return, the plants provide the bacteria with carbohydrates produced through photosynthesis. This relationship significantly benefits the plant by improving nitrogen levels in the soil, reducing the need for synthetic fertilizers and enhancing crop yields.

text: Impact on Plant Production: | The presence of Rhizobium in the soil increases soil fertility and enhances the growth of leguminous crops. Farmers who use inoculants (products containing Rhizobium) often report healthier crops with higher yields and better resistance to pests. Furthermore, nitrogen-fixing legumes can improve soil health, which benefits subsequent crops grown in the same soil. | Key Takeaway: | Beneficial microorganisms like Rhizobium can help farmers achieve sustainable farming by improving soil health, reducing input costs, and boosting crop productivity. Their role in nitrogen fixation is a critical part of sustainable agriculture systems. | Case Study 1: Beneficial Microorganisms - Rhizobium Bacteria
